notes: \cpara{Tells how the author's grand-uncle, at his mother's funeral after her long decline, said God had taken her back piece by piece, ending with her smile.}

\cpara{The premise of the whole post: Jews ``usually'' avoid attributing tragedy to God. It is stated as a fact about a religion and supported by nothing. Jewish law says the opposite (see the notes on the Mishnah and on Maimonides).}

\cpara{The grand-uncle's words were a eulogy for his mother, spoken ``choking back tears.'' The post treats them as a statement of theology, evidence for a theory of religious self-deception, and two paragraphs later the basis of a prediction about his faith. It does not consider that a grieving son at a funeral may not be committing himself to a doctrine. (The grand-uncle's later departure makes the author's reading possible too.)}

\cfact{False about Jewish practice. The Mishnah (Berakhot 9:5) rules: ``One is obligated to recite a blessing for the bad that befalls him just as he recites a blessing for the good.'' For bad tidings the blessing is ``Blessed \ldots\ the true Judge'' (Berakhot 9:2). Jews say it on hearing of a death, and immediate family say it at the funeral as they tear their clothes. Attributing a death to God is not avoided in Judaism. It is prescribed, for the mourner, at the funeral: the occasion the post describes.}

\cfact{One view, presented as ``Jewish theology.'' Maimonides rejected it: ``I do not believe that it is through the interference of Divine Providence that a certain leaf drops [from a tree]'' (\textsc{Guide for the Perplexed} III:17, Friedländer's translation). He held that individual providence extends, among earthly creatures, only to human beings. The question the post treats as settled doctrine is disputed within the tradition.}

\cpara{``As I understood them'' is the only qualification the post puts on its theory of religion, and the theory is contradicted by the liturgy (previous notes). The surprise records what the author did not know about the practice, not what the grand-uncle was doing.}
\cpara{A prediction made after the fact: one relative, one outcome, and a theory fitted to both. Had the grand-uncle stayed, the anecdote would not be here.}

\cpara{The claim of uniqueness is hedged (``I have ever heard of''), and the paragraph's own example is not unique. Reconciling the days of Genesis with cosmic time is common in Christian apologetics too: ``day-age'' creationism reads the days as long ages, and the astronomer Hugh Ross founded a ministry, Reasons to Believe, to defend it.}
\cpara{Claims the tradition does allow inquiry, but attacks only points it means to defend and knows it can.}

\cpara{A slogan that is true of any community with a shared belief. Those who doubt successfully leave, so those who remain are those who did not. That is a selection effect, and the paragraph presents it as a rule of the religion.}

\cpara{``I expect,'' then ``probably went something like this,'' then an interior monologue the author wrote. The typical Orthodox doubt is invented and then shown to be shallow. No Orthodox Jew is quoted anywhere in the post.}
\cpara{The post picks the plague of the firstborn. It does not engage a single Jewish reading of the passage, though it will concede that there are ``a dozen'' (see the note there).}

\cpara{A compliment that sets up a story, and the story is false. The post says the old rabbis spilled wine to mark the Egyptians' suffering, and could afford the sympathy because ``Science was weaker in these days.'' Both halves fail (see notes).}

\cfact{Incomplete on the count and wrong on the history. The usual custom is sixteen drops: one for each plague, and six more for other words of the text. The earliest source, a sermon of Rabbi Eleazar of Worms (c.~1176--1238), ties the drops to ``the sword of the Holy One, blessed be He, which has sixteen sides,'' and says the custom ``teaches us that we will not be injured'': it wards off harm. The reading about the Egyptians' suffering originated with an Orthodox rabbi in the 1800s, and its earliest written source is a lecture by Eduard Baneth published in 1904 (Zvi Ron, ``Our Own Joy is Lessened and Incomplete,'' \textsc{Hakirah} 19). The sympathy the post credits to rabbis of a pre-scientific age belongs to rabbis of the nineteenth and twentieth centuries. The post's explanation, that weak science let the old rabbis afford compassion, has the dates backwards.}

\clogic{The Talmud comes closer than the post allows. In Megillah 10b, God silences the angels at the Red Sea: ``The work of My hands, the Egyptians, are drowning at sea, and you wish to say songs?'' It concerns the sea, not the firstborn, and it rebukes rejoicing rather than the act. But it is the tradition confronting the harshness the post says it never asks about.}

\cpara{A claim about what Orthodox Jews do not ask, with no evidence, followed by three replies they supposedly never need, the last (``Murdering babies is okay when God does it!'') written for them by the author. Three paragraphs later the post grants that there are ``probably a dozen'' replies to the objection. A dozen replies means people asked.}

\cpara{The thesis, a causal claim about why educated believers stay religious, resting on ``I suspect'' and one family anecdote. No rival explanation is considered: family, community, practice, identity. The last is the author's own theory from ``Belief as Attire,'' two months earlier, which holds that belonging to a tribe produces passion that belief alone cannot.}

\cpara{Whoever thinks of the slaughtered son ``is \emph{really} questioning it, and is probably not going to stay Jewish much longer.'' Because of ``probably,'' a believer who thinks of it and stays counts against the claim, so it can be tested in principle. The post offers no test, and the only evidence is one relative.}

\cpara{The post's own method, turned on the post. The closing advice is to ``Ask yourself what \emph{smart} people who disagree would say to your first reply, and your second reply.'' Here the author has an objection to Judaism, grants that there are ``a dozen'' replies, and examines none. The method is applied to the family's belief, and the author's own critique of it is exempted.}

\cpara{``More than anything'' ranks one cause above all others without naming the others. The claim that avoidance is ``not a matter of training, but a matter of instinct'' has no evidence. The paragraph also moves from ``religion'' to ``their beliefs'' in general. The general claim is the one the reader is meant to take away, and it has been argued, weakly, only for religion.}
\cpara{Advises deliberately confronting the most painful objection to a cherished belief, asking what smart opponents would say to each reply, and reciting a passage on facing the truth.}
\cpara{The Gendlin passage again, now a text to recite under pain. See the notes on ``You Can Face Reality'' for its source and its original setting, a book section on people helping each other.}
